title: 'Hundreds and hundreds of bones': In a hidden Alpine cave, a mountaineer discovers an Ice Age cave bear graveyard
content:
The BBC reveals exclusive images from inside a previously uncharted cave in the Dolomites, containing a trove of skeletons from huge, long-extinct cave bears – offering a rare window into the Ice Age.
Mountain guide Kurt Walde was on a near-vertical slope in the Italian Dolomites, at an altitude of a little over 2,850m (9,350ft), searching for an uncharted cave.
Descending from the mountain summit down a slope littered with loose rock, Walde reached a ledge that he thought would be the cave. It was a false hope.
"At that moment I felt a bit desperate," says Walde. "I continued to downclimb. Eventually , I reached the end of my rope."
Walde was convinced he was close. He hadn't been feeling well that morning, but had donned his 22kg (50lb) backpack anyway. For the last few metres, he dispensed with his rope, and reached the cave's entrance without it.
Inside was an extraordinary sight. Deep in the cave, the glow of his head lamp fell across a graveyard of Ice Age skeletons. They are suspected to belong to Ursus ladinicus , a species of cave bear that went extinct around 24,000 years ago.
Scroll down to see the first images taken inside the cave and sketches of its layout by Walde, shared with the BBC.
The entrance to the newly discovered cave lies across the mountain from another famous site, the Conturines cave, in the Fanes-Senes-Braies Natural Park in northern Italy. So far, that is the only place where Ursus ladinicus remains have been confirmed.
The cave bears found in Conturines weighed around 1,200kg (2,650lb) and were 3m (10ft) long, with males larger than females. Their teeth suggest that they were exclusively plant-eaters, feeding on Alpine herbs, leaves and tougher grasses.
The discovery of Conturines in 1987 transformed what we knew about Ice Age cave bears. Nearly 40 years later, the discovery of this sister cave means our understanding could be set to change once again.
Walde, from the nearby city of Brunico in South Tyrol, has always believed that there is more to Conturines than meets the eye. Walde has been a mountain guide for 41 years, and is one of only two guides to the famous cave.
"During all [those] tours, I always had a feeling that this cave is not all there is to it," says Walde. "I thought there must be something more."
Three and a half years ago, while he was on a peak, Walde spotted a black mark on the mountainside, creating a striking contrast to the lunar-like surroundings.
"That was the first sign," Walde says. Convinced there was something interesting there, he decided one day he would brave the vertiginous slope to get there. "I have to go and see it up close."
In July 2026, Walde finally made up his mind to explore the site, and was met with a treasure trove of ancient remains.
On entering, he was struck by the topographic similarities between this cavern and the Conturines cave.
"I immediately thought this den must be part of a cave system," he says. Ecstatic at having safely entered, "I wanted to extend this moment and feeling as long as possible", he says. He compares it to receiving a gift and wanting to extend the suspense before opening it.
The first 60m (200ft) or so of the cave are a straight line, reaching a large speleothem – a natural mineral deposit – at the end of that stretch. Nearby, he found a solitary bone lying on an elevated bedrock formation resembling a table. The arrangement struck him as "mysterious".
From that point onwards, the cave descends to the left. It was here that Walde came across numerous bones and skulls.
"That was very exciting," says Walde. "I really did my best to control my emotions."

The finding of a hidden Alpine cave containing a trove of skeletons from huge, long-extinct cave bears is a substantial development in the field of paleontology, offering new insights into the lives of these ancient creatures.

title: 'Root cause’ of nationwide ground stop is unknown, FAA says
content: The root cause of the longest halt in flight departures to U.S. airports since 9/11 remains unclear after a Saturday press conference by U.S. transportation officials. Routers and networking equipment appeared to be involved in the technological disruption that grounded flights across the country, but a definitive cause has not been established as of Saturday afternoon. The inability to pinpoint the reason for the infrastructure malfunctions led the Federal Aviation Administration to take actions that resulted in the grounding order, Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration, told reporters. "Because of our lack of identifying the root cause, we were unwilling to take any risk that this propagation could actually result in a sensor losing connectivity with aircraft," he said. "What we saw was instability. We couldn't explain the instability," Bedford added. Officials reported issues with routers and networking equipment on Saturday, citing products and services from Cisco and L3Harris Technologies . "Until I can build [the new architecture], I'm stuck with L3Harris, who owns this network," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. In a statement on X, L3Harris said that it, in partnership with other tech companies, has completed more than 70% of the planned airspace communications conversion from legacy copper wires to a fiber-optic system. "We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously." On Friday, Duffy and Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin called for an air travel overhaul, with Duffy requesting $50 billion from Congress. FAA administrator Bedford said that router updates were a matter of regular business for his agency and distinct from modernization allocations. "We are constantly replacing 2,000, you know, Cisco 600 routers with Juniper routers, right? So this is ordinary course of business stuff. This is not part of the … FAA $12.5 billion modernization efforts. So let's not conflate those two things," Bedford said.

The topic is relevant to a specific category (science and technology) and provides new information that justifies publication.

content: Evidence of a rare particle decay fits physics’ best theory, giving scientists a new way to test whether our understanding of matter leaves something out. After more than 40 years of searching, physicists have found the first evidence of a particle decay predicted to occur only about once in every 10 billion beauty particles. The signal, recorded by the upgraded LHCb experiment at CERN’s Large Hadron Collider (LHC), offers a way to look for undiscovered particles through the influence they might have on that exceptionally unlikely event. Inside the protons and neutrons at an atom’s center are smaller building blocks called up and down quarks. Beauty quarks are heavier members of the same family, produced in huge numbers when particles collide at the LHC, and they exist for only around one and a half trillionths of a second before decaying. LHCb studies particles containing these short-lived quarks. In the decay at the center of the new result, known as Bd to mu mu , one such particle transforms into two muons, particles similar to electrons but heavier. With a statistical significance of 3.2 sigma, the signal is strong enough to qualify as evidence of the decay, although more data will be needed to reach the five-sigma threshold required to claim a discovery in particle physics. Professor Chris Parkes, head of the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Manchester, said, “This decay is remarkably unlikely, the chance of it happening is roughly like going on a romantic date and, on your very first try, finding the one perfect match for you among everyone on Earth.” An undiscovered particle could change the chances of a beauty particle decaying in a particular way, giving physicists a means of detecting its influence even if they cannot observe it directly at the LHC. The rarer a decay is, the more sensitive it can be to such effects. Researchers can therefore look for discrepancies between the measured decay rate and the predictions of the Standard Model, their best current theory of fundamental particles and their interactions. The new measurement matches those predictions, and greater precision could help reveal where the theory might eventually begin to break down. By pursuing these increasingly precise measurements, physicists hope to probe what they call the “Zeptoverse,” an unexplored world at distances of a zeptometer, or a billionth of a trillionth of a meter, where unknown particles and forces may be hiding. Professor Conor Fitzpatrick of the University of Manchester, deputy physics coordinator of the international LHCb collaboration, said, “There has been a more than forty year long search by physicists worldwide to observe this decay. It is a golden channel to observe the effects of new physics from beyond our current knowledge. “The results from this experiment are expanding our understanding of nature at its most fundamental level. We are excited to have finally seen this elusive signal and looking forward to the future discoveries that will come from our data.” Just five millimeters, or about 0.2 inches, from the LHC beams sits the Vertex Locator, a silicon pixel detector that tracks the paths of particles emerging from collisions with extreme precision. This major UK-built component is part of the upgraded LHCb experiment. University of Manchester researchers played key roles in the experiment and its upgrade, including developing detector technology that helped make the measurement possible. Dr. Stefano De Capua, who led construction of the detectors at the University of Manchester, said, “We worked with nearly 90 UK companies to construct this detector and trained the next generation of scientists and engineers on the novel technologies we are using. It is these detectors that we use to locate where the beauty meson was produced and pinpoint where it decayed into two muons.” Parkes led the international LHCb collaboration through construction of the upgrade and led its approval of the new result. Made a Fellow of the Royal Society earlier this year for his work on LHCb, he said, “The upgraded LHCb was a major undertaking – a fifteen-year design and construction project from a 1900 international member collaboration. “The UK made the largest nation contribution to the project, pioneering new technologies that have made today’s result possible, where we probe nature at a new scale. But this is also just the start, we are planning the construction of an experiment that will exploit the capabilities of the next-generation High Luminosity LHC, probing physics at an even smaller scale.” By collecting data at up to five times its previous rate, the upgraded experiment is expected to build a much larger dataset into the early 2030s. A further planned upgrade could increase that rate by another factor of ten, enabling more precise measurements of these decays and increasing sensitivity to undiscovered particles at even shorter distances. Professor Brian Cox, a particle physicist at the University of Manchester who was not involved in the experiment, said, “This is an important result and a beautiful example of how science advances. We upgrade our instruments and we see nature in greater detail. Occasionally we see something we don’t understand, and then progress is made. We cannot know whether this progress will be incremental or genuinely world-changing – that’s science! LHCb is a major scientific success.” The experiment is funded by the Science and Technology Facilities Council as part of UK Research and Innovation.
